newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: US urges Milosevic to hand over war crime suspects.
newsitem.headline: US urges Milosevic to hand over war crime suspects.

text.p: A U.S. envoy to former Yugoslavia pressed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday to comply with the Dayton peace accord and hand over indicted war criminals to justice.

"I talked about the war crimes issue in great detail, including the need for indicted war criminals to be sent to The Hague to be tried," Ambassador Bob Gelbard told reporters after meeting Milosevic in Belgrade.
His brief visit to Belgrade comes less than a week before Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is due in the Balkans.
U.S. sources said they believed positive results of Gelbard's talks in Belgrade could pave the way for her visit to the Yugoslav capital, but refused to give details.

Belgrade refuses to hand over three senior Yugoslav army officers indicted by the war crimes court in The Hague in connection with atrocities in the Croatian town of Vukovar during the six-month Croatian-Serb war in 1991.

Four years since it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, the tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminals, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, who remain at large like the majority of other suspects.

So far only nine have been arrested and sent to The Hague, including Bosnian Croat prison camp commander Zlatko Aleksovski. Croatia handed him over last month only after the United States threatened to block major loans to the country.

Albright has said a priority of the new U.S. initiative to reinvigorate international peace efforts in Bosnia is greater support for the war crimes tribunal, which she plans to visit in The Hague on Wednesday.

Albright has said Washington will bring increased financial and other pressures to bear to encourage parties to the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accords -- including Croatia and Serbia as well as the Bosnian factions -- to comply with their commitments.
Many experts see a deepening crisis in Bosnia.

U.S. officials acknowledge that while the Dayton accord ended the Bosnian war, the peace is not secure with signatories resisting integration, return of refugees and cooperation with the war crimes tribunal.
Gelbard also said Milosevic had to help in getting Bosnian Serbs sent to The Hague for trial.

"We have been pressing all the parties to do this, recently we pressed successfully for Croatia to send Zlatko Aleksovksi to The Hague and we consider this to be one of our very highest priorities. This is an issue that will not go away, this is extremely important," the U.S. envoy said.
Gelbard said his talks with Milosevic also focused "at great length" on the need for full compliance with the Dayton agreements.
"Serbia and President Milosevic in particular have a strong responsibility for ensuring full compliance of those agreements and we discussed those issues at great length," he said.

The United States has retained some sanctions against Belgrade pending resolution of the war crime issue, compliance with the Dayton accord and improvement of human rights in Serbia's troubled ethnic Albanian-majority province of Kosovo.

Gelbard said he and Milosevic also talked about "Kosovo issues related to the need to work for further steps to ensure full democracy and consolidation of democracy, including freedom of expression in the country".
